summary: CogAdapt takes an existing EEG and eye-tracking dataset (37 participants reading 32 Java programs) and turns it into priors that weight training examples and tokens. Combined with the frozen model's per-task block responses, these priors choose about 6 of 47-48 transformer blocks to LoRA-tune per training example in two MoE code models (Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, GLM-4.7-Flash). On LiveCodeBench (175 tasks) it reaches 29.71% vs 18.86% for all-block fine-tuning (Qwen) and 24.00% vs 17.71% (GLM); BigCodeBench gains are 1-3 points. Each condition is a single generation pass, no un-fine-tuned base model is reported, and there are no significance tests.

claims.claim: Human reading responses and MoE computation correlate at the same code regions (75.0-83.3% of regions positive)
claims.evidence: Figure 4: median Spearman 0.18-0.24 with resampling intervals that account for participants and programs; the EEG-Qwen interval reaches 0.000. 81 regions over 32 Java programs.

claims.claim: CogAdapt achieves the best pass@1 on LiveCodeBench and BigCodeBench, +10.86 and +6.29 points over matched regular fine-tuning on LiveCodeBench
claims.evidence: Table 1: single pass per condition; on 175 LCB tasks the gains are 19 and 11 tasks; BigCodeBench gains are +1.37 (3 of 220 tasks) for Qwen and +3.18 for GLM; ties No-Gaze on Qwen-BCB. No untuned base is reported, so the all-block baseline may simply be degrading the model; no significance test despite the section title 'Statistical Comparison'.

claims.claim: Ablations show both block selection and human guidance contribute
claims.evidence: Table 1: All-Block, Rand-K6, Model-Only, No-EEG and No-Gaze fall below the full method in most cells, by 0-6 tasks; Rand-K6 is the only condition with variance (SD 0.57-1.51 over 3 masks).
Table 2: 3.32-3.73M vs 25.95-27.06M parameters is straightforward accounting; wall-clock time falls only 2.5-5.9% and GPU energy 2.1-4.6% because the full backbone still runs forward.

patterns.note: Task-dependent sparse LoRA beats all-block LoRA and fixed CKA-selected blocks on the same data, but results are single-pass, no untuned base is reported, and differences are a few tasks on 175/220-task test sets.
Uses developers' comprehension measurements (EEG, eye tracking) as a training signal for models; it does not measure or protect developers' own comprehension.

methodology.sample: Human data: 37 participants, 32 Java programs, 81 semantic regions (NoviceVsExpert corpus). Training: 534 LiveCodeBench v1-4 Python solutions; BigCodeBench split 760 train / 160 dev / 220 test. Evaluation: 175 LiveCodeBench v6 tasks and 220 BigCodeBench tasks.
methodology.baselines: Regular FT (all blocks, same LoRA and router settings) and CKA-K6 fixed sparse selection; no untuned base model and no other PEFT or layer-selection baselines such as LISA or AdaLoRA.
methodology.variance: Single generation pass per condition; SD only for Rand-K6 over three masks; no training seeds and no significance tests.
methodology.contamination_controls: LiveCodeBench v6 evaluation separated from v1-4 training data; pretraining contamination not discussed.
methodology.languages: Human data in Java; training and evaluation in Python.

standards.peer_review: arXiv preprint (ACM template with placeholder conference)
standards.artifacts: No code, priors, masks or checkpoints released

biases.detail: The only dense baseline is all-block LoRA on 534 examples; without the untuned model's score, gains may reflect less forgetting rather than better adaptation.
Single generation pass and single training run per condition.
175 and 220 test tasks, so one task is 0.57 or 0.45 points; the EEG prior is a ridge regression fitted to 32 programs.
The program-level 'EEG prior' is a ridge regression from eight static code metrics (length, nesting, operator and call counts), i.e. a code-complexity weighting presented as cognition.
Code-generation evaluation is Python only; the human data are Java.

coi.detail: Academic authors; open-weight models from third parties.

verdict_reason: A reasonable ablation design on two MoE models, but every number is one generation pass on small test sets, the untuned base is missing (so the all-block baseline may be a strawman), the human 'EEG prior' reduces to static complexity metrics, and nothing is released. It is a model-training paper with no bearing on harness design, admitted at low weight in line with other code-model training papers.
applicability: None for the discovery and onboarding harness. It is a fine-tuning technique for teams that train MoE code models, and the team uses hosted models through agent hosts. Despite the developer-learning topic hit, it does not study developer comprehension, onboarding or deskilling; it reuses developers' EEG and eye-tracking data as a training signal for models.
